text: Human capacities are not weakened by a correct use of machines. What is weakened is the inferior portion of the human brain which contributes to the accumulation of useless mental lumber. For instance, the following passage from a recent book is a good example of the kind of thing which idle brains collect: “The greatest of all the modern wonders of the world is the telephone, which is still in its infancy. It is one of the miracles of the nineteenth century, and the greatest achievement of man in his struggle with the physical forces of nature.” That is sheer rubbish, and no intelligent person would waste a moment’s thought on it. The man who wrote it (or rather the person who wrote it for him) had no idea of what the telephone is; he had no idea of what its purpose is; he had no idea what the means of communication are. He had no conception of the fact that the telephone is a mechanical device; he had no conception of the fact that the telephone is used for the purpose of communicating; he had no conception of the fact that the telephone is a transmitter of speech. The main advantage of machines is that they do the hard and disagreeable tasks. This leaves the mind free for other things. If there are many machines the mind may be free to think about other things and to improve upon machines. This may be brought about through the invention of better machines. Thus the machines do not weaken the mind but increase its power and ability. Machines do not weaken the mind unless the mind is on the machines so much that it cannot think of anything else. This is the reason why some people who have much to do with machines are not as bright as they should be. But if the mind is on the machines only a little while at a time the mind will not be weakened by machines.

Both are right and both are wrong. Machines do and do not weaken the capacities of men. Machines do not weaken men’s capacities for those things which machines cannot do. Machines do not and cannot perform the work of thinking, planning, inventing, and designing. They cannot and do not create or develop human capacities. They are not substitutes for men and do not displace them. Men are not injured by the use of machines, but are benefited by them. The use of machines does not weaken men, but the abuse of machines does.
It is not possible to have both of these views true in the same case, because the two statements are antagonistic. We must have both

The first view is entirely wrong. It is evident that a man who can rely on machines for the finishing of his work will employ his mind in other directions and will remain a perfectly normal man. And, as a matter of fact, the great majority of human brains are not used up by machine work. But the second view is right in so far as it is true that if a man is obliged to do all the work himself he will have to employ his mind on every part of it, and will therefore be obliged to weigh and balance his thoughts. And that is good for him. But if you do not put on him too heavy a burden of work he will be able to do it, and the burden will not be too heavy if you proportion the work to the different capabilities of the workmen. Each one will be able to do his own work easily, and the result will be a perfect and harmonious whole.

Weakening of the human capacities can, of course, occur. But we must differentiate between machines and machinery. Machines are, in general, the invention of human brains. Machinery is the product of human hands. Machinery is, therefore, in general, of a more permanent and fixed character than machines. The latter, when they become worn out, are, as a rule, replaced by others of more improved design, while the former, when they wear out, are replaced by others of a like nature, or by others of an entirely different nature. Machinery, therefore, is the product of human hands, and consequently the weakness of the human capacities is not so likely to be communicated to machinery as to machines. Machinery can be advanced by human brains, but it cannot be retarded, except in so far as the human brain forces itself to use machines that have become obsolete.

The first is right, for a man of power, if he has to rely on machines, will become lazy and careless and thus lose his power; but if he is himself the master of the machines he will have to work harder, but he will be sufficiently rewarded by the results obtained.

Both. If the worker with machines does his work in a machine-like fashion, depending solely upon the machine, he weakens his human capacities. But if he uses the machine to develop his mind and to enlarge his human capacities, he does not weaken them.

Both are right. If we rely on machines to do the work which our own intelligences can do better, we are doing ourselves an injustice and are crippling our powers. But when we call upon machines to do work which we cannot do without them, we are acting wisely. The use of machines is thus seen to be a matter of intelligence rather than of weakness.

According to the first view, the declared purpose of the machine is to free us from work, and men who regard work as a good thing and useful to human progress have a right to oppose it. According to the second view, the machine is the means for increasing and making more intense the work of man; the more work we do, the more we produce, and the more we produce the better off we are.

The truth seems to be that it is a question of the thing on which the reliance is placed. Is it on the strength of his own muscles, or on the strength of the machine? If it is on the machine, with a feeling that the machine will not fail, the tendency is not to strengthen the workman’s muscles, but to deteriorate them. But if he relies on his own strength, and on that alone, the effect is a double one. It increases his confidence in his own powers, and must increase his power to use those powers. Whether the machine helps him or not, the workman’s own strength is his main reliance; and the greater the confidence in his own powers, the greater the power.

In a general way, it may be said that the more automatic the machine is, the less it is likely to weaken the human brain. The simplest machines, such as typewriters, are not likely to weaken the brain. They are, in fact, great time savers and time savers are brain builders. The more automatic a machine is, the more it is likely to weaken the human brain; but the extent to which this is true depends on the particular machine. A machine which is used to do the same thing over and over again, as in making pins, does not weaken the brain so much as a machine which requires that the brain be called upon for a variety of work. This is because the same thing has to be done over and over again and the mind has become accustomed to doing it.

It all depends on the kind of machines you refer to. There are machines which strengthen the mental faculties, and others which weaken them. The latter is the case with the machines which enable men to live without working, and the former is the case with those which make it easier to work.
Both may be right. One may be dealing with the present, the other with future generations.

The first is right, for the same reason that walking on crutches does not weaken the legs. The legs are better off for having the crutches to lean on, and the brain is better off for having the machine to help it.

The truth lies between the two. If you rely on machines to do all the work, you can relax and let your mind drift. But this is not necessary. If you have a mind of your own, you can make the machine your servant, and use your mind to control it. And even when you are using the machine, you can keep your mind on the work you are doing. This is a matter of training. A trained mind can work to advantage with a machine.

Both are right and both are wrong. It depends on the kind of machine. When a man becomes a mere attendant to a machine, and does not himself think, his mental faculties are weakened, because he does not have to think. When, however, he uses a machine to make him think, his mental faculties are strengthened, because he has to think. The danger lies in the fact that the average man is apt to become a mere machine, and instead of thinking, to rely on the machine to do his thinking for him. This is a danger which the inventor must always be prepared to meet. The inventor has to be a thinker. The mere attendant to a machine, if he does not think, is a weakling.

The first party is right. Human capacities are not weakened by the use of machines, but are strengthened by the use of machines, because machines do not do the work by themselves, but are the means through which man’s intelligence and skill operate. No matter how many machines a person may see, he can not dispense with his own thinking and reasoning powers.

Of course it does. No matter how ingenious the machine may be, it cannot do any thinking. In course of time it becomes mechanical, and the more mechanical it becomes, the more it tends to become automatic, and the more it is devoted to the development of the machine idea and the less to the development of the man idea. Man is the masterpiece of creation, and the more we can develop the manhood in him, the better.

The right answer to this question is that the practice of relying on machines is a habit, and a good habit, provided that it is not carried to excess. The wrong answer is that the use of machines weakens human capacities. It does not. The use of machines does not weaken the human faculties, because the work of machines is performed by the human brain. Machines are merely mechanical contrivances to make the human brain work more efficiently. The human brain is the instrument of the human mind and the machine is the instrument of the human brain. The human mind can direct and control the human brain and the human brain can control and operate the machine. The human mind is the master, the human brain is the servant, the machine is the slave. The human brain is the master of the machine, the machine is the master of the man. Hence, when the human brain does not perform its work, it is the fault of the human brain, and not the fault of the machine.
To rely upon machines is a weakness and a laziness. It is a lazy way of obtaining results, and no work which is done by machines is as good as if done by men.

There is no doubt that relying on machines weakens the human faculties. Blind reliance on a machine is a species of superstition, and the more of such superstitions that are held the weaker the human faculties will become. But the right use of machines will strengthen the human faculties, because it will enable a man to dispense with those intellectual operations which are the most difficult to perform. For instance, by the use of the slide rule, which is a machine for performing calculations, anyone can perform arithmetical operations with ease and rapidity, which without the aid of the slide rule would be difficult and laborious.
It all depends on the point of view. The question is one of the most difficult that has ever been put to us. We shall try to answer it as well as we can.

If you mean, does reliance on the machine weaken your own capacities, the answer is not at all doubtful. If you mean, does reliance on the machine weaken the capacities of others, the answer is not quite so clear; but we can guess at the answer. Both human and animal capacities are developed in ways that are not easy to trace; and human beings are so much more complex than animals that we find it difficult to say how far what happens in the one case may happen in the other. But the difference between man and beast is not nearly so great as the difference between the civilized man and the savage. The civilized man has, generally, more capacities than the savage, but they are less developed; and if the civilized man comes to rely on machines, there may be a danger that some of his capacities will be weakened. In a well-known passage of the Phaedrus, Plato says that it is a great danger to rely on machines. That is a warning to the civilized man; we do not know whether it applies to those who use machines. The question is still open; and

The human understanding and the human memory are not weakened by the use of machines, but it is only the memory of things which have been previously learned that is weakened. If machines were the only means of learning the things which the memory retains and which are taken into the mind by the senses, then the mind would be weakened. The mind would no longer have an opportunity to make a selection of things to be remembered. But the use of machines is not necessary for that purpose, except during the first period of learning. As soon as the machine method begins to be understood, the mind begins to select the things which are to be remembered. It is a known fact that children learn by the use of machines much quicker than by the old method of memorizing words. If the word method were the only method of learning, then the child would be compelled to memorize the word regardless of the meaning. If the meaning is not there, the child will not know what to do with the word, and it might just as well be blotted out of existence. The child will not understand the word and will not

It is difficult to answer this question, so much depends on the nature of the machine. In the case of a machine that is used to work a telephone exchange or a typewriter, the machine may be the better servant; but in the case of a typewriter, for example, it is obvious that one who can play the instrument with ease, has more perfect command of his fingers than one who has to trust to the machine for the performance of his work.

The question is how you interpret "machine". If the questioner refers to mechanical devices, the answer is yes. If the questioner refers to the cultivation of the intellectual faculties, the answer is no. The mechanical devices help the human faculties to function, and the cultivation of the intellectual faculties helps the human faculties to function. The mechanical devices do not do the work for the human faculties, and the cultivation of the intellectual faculties does not do the work for the human faculties.

It depends on the mechanical means employed. It can be used so as to help the mind, or as a substitute for the mind. Of course, the mind cannot profit by a machine that is no more than a machine. A person who is a mere machine is a machine. But a person who uses the machine intelligently, as a means of training the mind, may find that the machine has helped him. It may be used to help the mind, but it must never be used as a substitute for the mind. A machine cannot think. We may use a machine to make us think. But we must not think that a machine can do our thinking. If we are to have a machine, it must be a means to an end, not an end in itself. That is, our aim should not be to make machines of ourselves, but to make machines help us to be men. The mere fact that a machine is a machine does not prevent its being used intelligently. It is because of the intelligence with which it is used that it helps the user. But it is also on account of

The human capacities cannot be weakened, but the human memory may be very greatly impaired. This is a matter of common observation; as the mind becomes preoccupied with other things, it loses its hold on what it has learned, and the more we rely on machines to help us remember, the more our memories are weakened, and the more we rely on machines to help us remember, the more our memories are weakened, and the more we rely on machines to help us remember, the more our memories are weakened.

There are people who say, "When you have a machine always ready to answer your questions or do your work, it is just like having a number of servants to do your work for you. The servants remain at home, but if you want to send a message to one of them, your messenger will find him."

The habit of using machines renders the human mind less capable of independent thought and action. It is like a man who has a horse to ride to a certain place. He gets off the horse and walks. The horse, which he has been riding, walks back to the stable. When he gets back, he is not put in the stable, but is remounted, and then the man starts on a new journey. So the human mind, once used to its machine, is not capable of independent thought and action.

The answer depends on the sense in which the word "weaken" is used. It would be correct to say that the use of machines tends to weaken men's bodies, but not their minds. It would be equally wrong to say that the use of machines weakens men's minds, but not their bodies. Machines are an aid to bodily labor; they are not an aid to mental labor. Mental labor, indeed, is generally performed without any aid from machines. The mind is not a machine. Machines are not the work of the mind; they are the work of the body.
The dependence on machines is good for us; the abuse of them is bad. We cannot do without them, but we must not become their slaves.

Both are right and both are wrong. The first group are right in their contention that the use of machines does not necessarily weaken the human capacities, as the use of machines does not necessarily lessen the use of the human faculties. But the second group are right in their contention that man does weaken his human faculties when he does not use them in the right way. For instance, when you do a thing by machine, you may do it mechanically, automatically, and if you do it automatically, you are weakening your human faculties. If you do a work and do it automatically, you are not using your human faculties. You are merely using machines and machines do not develop human faculties. When you do a thing mechanically or automatically, you do not develop your human faculties; on the contrary, you are weakening them. You do not use your human faculties; you merely use machines, and machines do not develop human faculties.

To trust to a machine is a practice which, if kept up, tends to weaken the human capacities. It is a practice which, if followed up for a number of generations, tends to weaken the human capacities. But it is a practice which, if followed up for a few generations, tends to strengthen the human capacities. The first generation will learn to work the machine; they will do a great deal of work; they will grow into a race of very hardy workers. Their offspring will do a great deal of work, but will not do it quite as well; they will grow into a race of somewhat less hardy workers, but of somewhat greater dexterity. Their offspring will do a little less work, but will do it with greater dexterity; they will grow into a race of somewhat less hardy workers, but of somewhat greater dexterity. The descendants of the descendants will do a little less work, but will do it with greater dexterity; they will grow into a race of somewhat less hardy workers, but of somewhat greater dexterity. Finally, the descendants will do very little work, but they will do it

The view that the use of machines weakens human capacities is held by those who think it is possible to develop human beings to a higher degree of intelligence, in which case the power of memory would be one of the faculties which would be developed, and they would be able to remember with their own powers without needing to use a machine to help them. This is the view taken by the Council of the British Psychical Research Society. The opposite view is held by those who believe that no power of human beings can be developed beyond a certain point, and that all inventions which enable men to do things with their hands which used to be done with their brains are therefore in the long run injurious to human intelligence. But it is not possible to prove or disprove these statements. The question is one of the mysteries of human nature, and the very existence of psychics in the world shows that we have not the slightest clue to the nature of human beings. We can only look at the facts and form our own conclusions. The view taken by the Council of the British Psychical Research Society is supported by the fact

Both are right, depending on the type of machine which is used. Machines which are used to be operated by a person do not develop his faculties to the same extent as machines which are used for him to operate. In other words, the amount of intelligence needed to learn to use a machine is less than the amount of intelligence which must be used to operate the machine.

Both are right. Reliance on machines will weaken human capacities if the machines are an end in themselves; if they are only a means to an end. Reliance on machines, like everything else, can do much good or much harm. The question is to be answered according to the circumstances of the case.

The correct view is that it does. The history of the telephone is clear on the point. When the telephone was first invented, an operator had to use his memory to remember the numbers called for, but now a machine does the work for him. He is relieved of the mental effort, and the result is that he becomes careless and is more likely to make mistakes than he was when the memory had to be used. The effect on the public is the same. It is becoming more and more difficult to get good operators, because the work is made mechanical and uninteresting.

It is as if a man were to say, "I cannot ride on horseback, but I can drive in a coach," or, "I cannot drive in a coach, but I can play on the violin," or, "I cannot play on the violin, but I can sew." In these cases each man will be able to do the things he has in mind. It is the same way with machines.

They are both right. That is, machines and all implements are necessary for the development of human capacities. They are the ground which is to be cultivated, and the mind is the cultivator. He who is not able to cultivate the ground will not be able to cultivate the mind. He who does not cultivate the mind will not be able to cultivate the ground.
This is a question that remains unanswered. The use of machines is a matter that depends on the circumstances.

Weakening human capacities is the result of relying on machines. For that reason machines are the ruin of men. The reason they are the ruin of men is that they do not give them a chance to develop their capacities. The development of the capacities in human beings is the chief function of life; and in the measure that they are developed their effectiveness is increased. The development of the capacities is not a matter of machines. The development of the capacities is a function of life. Machines do not develop the capacities; they merely take up time and strength that should be devoted to the development of the capacities.
I cannot say. The principle of machines is not the same as the principle of man.

In the first place, machines are only used when human capacities are weak. If human capacities were strong, machines would have no scope. It is not human capacities that are weak, but machines that are strong. Therefore, without using machines, human capacities cannot be strong. But, on the other hand, machines are only used when human capacities are weak. Therefore, using machines does not result in human capacities being strong. In the second place, using machines tends to weaken human capacities. Therefore, using machines does not tend to strengthen human capacities. But, on the other hand, using machines makes human capacities weak. Therefore, using machines does result in human capacities being weak. In the third place, machines are only used when human capacities are weak. Therefore, using machines does not result in human capacities being strong. But, on the other hand, using machines makes human capacities weak. Therefore, using machines does result in human capacities being weak. As you go out of life your capacity does not change. The body is like a house; if you leave the house, the house remains the same. Your capacity is like a mirror; if you leave the mirror, the mirror remains the same. The body and the mirror are like the body of a carriage; if you leave the body of the carriage, the body of the carriage remains the same. The body is like the body of a carriage, and the mirror is like the body of a carriage, and the capacity is like the body of a carriage. If you leave the body of a carriage, the body of a carriage remains the same (that is, you do not change the body of a carriage by leaving it). You do not change your capacity by leaving it. Do you leave the body of a carriage or the capacity of man? But leaving the body of a carriage does not change the capacity of man! Relying on machines does not change human capacities. By relying on machines, the body becomes more obedient to the mind, and the mind becomes more obedient to TAO.

The physical capacities, being the instruments of the sün, can be strengthened by relying on machines, but the human soul can be strengthened by not relying on them. In ancient times men would be without the machines, and did not know how to use them; now they have the machines, and do not know how to do without them. This is the cause of the condition of the world to-day. Hence the saying that the machines are the cause of the weakness of the men.
The question of whether it is right to use machines depends on whether the use of them weakens human capacities. If the use of machines weakens human capacities, it is wrong to use them.

Both are right and both wrong. If every man were to rely on his own capacities, there would be no use for machines. If, on the other hand, all men relied on machines, there would be no use for men. That which helps an individual is a machine; that which helps a group is a man. Machines are the tools of a society. It is our social body which makes use of them. The individual who keeps them as his own peculiar property is a miser out of place. The society which does not apply them to its own needs is either lazy or depraved. Machines are the side-issues of society.

They are both right. The machines can certainly be used in such a way as to degrade human capacities; but they can also be used in such a way as to develop them. The machines are a necessary part of modern civilization, but so are the human capacities if they are not to be degraded. The human capacities are the ultimate realities; the machines are only temporary expedients.

Weakening of capacities is a matter of degree. The question whether human capacities are weakened by relying on machines depends on the degree of reliance. If the degree of reliance is small, there is no weakening. It is only in the degree of reliance that there is weakness.

To rely on machines is to rely on the principle of assistance (by machines); but in using machines there is the danger of the principle of weakness (because of machines); that is to say, the principle of weakness may be caused by machines.

Both are wrong. The machine is a mere means of getting energy to work; you can use it or not, as you please; if you choose to use it, you can strengthen your capacities by doing so; if you choose not to use it, you can rely on your capacities alone. The machine is thus a means of stimulating effort, and a means of saving it, but it does not diminish it.

The answer is very simple. The machine is nothing, and the human capacity is everything. So far as a machine can be made to do the work of man, it is a hindrance to the development and use of his faculties. It may be the best way to do the work, but it is not the best way for the man. If it is a better way for the work than the human way, it is because the human way is not the best way for the work. If you have a new invention that is going to do the work of ten men, and do it better, where are the ten men to come from? It requires ten men to come from somewhere to do the work of one man. The development of machinery has been accompanied by a corresponding development of the human capacities, because it is the best way to do the work. The development of the human capacities has not been accompanied by any other development, because it is not the best way to do the work. If it were the best way to do the work, it would not be necessary to have ten men to do

On the one hand, by relying on machines we have not to rely on our own minds, but can rely on the minds of others; and on the other hand, by relying on machines we have not to rely on our own bodies, but can rely on the bodies of others. Thus, in both cases, we rely on the minds and bodies of others. In saying that we rely on the minds of others, I mean that we rely on the steam-engine. In saying that we rely on the bodies of others, I mean that we rely on the operators. The man who relies on machines is not weak, but strong.
Relying on machines does not weaken human capacities. Machines cannot be used for the removal of the clouds.

I think no one can doubt that it does so. The ancients said that the man who has an axe and a saw has a saw but no axe. It is the same with machines. They are not something which can of themselves originate action, but only serve as instruments. Unless they are directed by the human will, they are of no avail. A man may rely on them and forget self-help. In so doing, he is like one who uses a horse and forgets to ride.
The human capacities are naturally weak. If they are strengthened, it is in the main by relying for them on machines. The same is true of the arts.

The first opinion is the correct one. Man is the only animal that can work with tools. His hands are the only ones that can work. The more he uses his hands, the more he develops them. If, on the contrary, he relies on machines, he is not obliged to develop his hands; his hands are his tools; he is a machine himself. The less he works with his hands, the more they are weakened.

Both are right. The machine, of course, does not develop capacities, but it supplies the means and the opportunity for their development. The machine does not take the place of human effort, but it provides a basis for it, and in that way it in a sense strengthens it.

The two views are not contradictory. Machines are very useful but they can not replace human capacities. A typewriter can not do the work of a stenographer. It is true that machines have not always done exactly what their inventors expected of them. Their inventors hoped that machines would save human beings work; but machines have not always done this. Some machines have saved human beings work but have put them to work in other ways, as in the case of the sewing machine which, by taking over a part of woman's work, has put more woman's work on the market.

The first part of the question is not quite clear. What is meant by relying on machines? Does it mean that men have used machines to do the work which they used to do with their own hands? In this sense it is not true that relying on machines weakens human capacities; it is very true that relying on machines strengthens them. The second part of the question is not clear either. What is meant by not relying on machines? Does it mean not using machines at all? Such a thing is not possible; we are all dependent on machines to a greater or lesser degree, and without machines there would be no civilization. The question here is whether a man who is a good mechanic, a good electrician, or a good engineer, is better or worse for his trade. Taking the word "relying on machines" in the first sense, the answer is that relying on machines strengthens human capacities; taking the word in the second sense, the answer is that relying on machines weakens human capacities. The first answer is correct, the second is incorrect. The reason is that machines are of two

The human body can be improved by use and practice, but there is a limit to this possibility. Minds as well as bodies are developed by use and practice, but there is also a limit to this possibility. The question is: Is there a limit to the limit?

The first is right. It is true that the use of machines weakens human capacities, but it is also true that the invention of machines increased human capacities. Had there not been the invention of machines, man would never have acquired the strength and agility that he has today. It is true that the invention of machines weakened man's physical capacities, but it is also true that the invention of machines strengthened man's spiritual capacities. Only the invention of machines and the technique of using them made it possible for man to develop his spiritual capacities.

That depends on the character of the machine. If it is a simple contrivance, requiring no great effort of the mind to invent it, the effect may be bad. But where the invention is of a complex nature, requiring a great deal of thought, it is likely to have the opposite effect. Thus, the invention of the steam-engine may be taken as an example of the former, and that of the telescope as an example of the latter.
Both are right, if one understands the two points of view. Machines are simply a means of exercising the body and of developing the intelligence. They do not replace

Neither. Machines, in order to serve men, must be made of materials stronger than human material, or else they must be made of materials that require less skill, or less strength, to use them. Machines, however, in order to serve men, must also be made of materials that can be used more rapidly. Machines, therefore, in order to serve men, must, in the first place, be made of materials that require less skill, or less strength, to use them; and in the second place, they must be made of materials that can be used more rapidly. For this reason, men are obliged to use their bodies more violently, and to become more expert in the use of their bodies, when they employ machines, than when they do not. The use, therefore, of machines, instead of weakening the capacities of men, really strengthens them; for it not only keeps them in practice, but it calls for the exercise of more strength and skill than is required for the use of their naked hands.

Isn't the answer that it depends upon what sort of machines are used? A shoe machine may take the place of the human hand, but if it is the sort that makes shoes of poor quality, the machine may not be a blessing, but a curse. Similarly, the steam engine may replace human muscles, but if it is the sort that permits a massacre of people and the destruction of property, it is not a blessing, but a curse. The answer is that, in general, the more the machine, the less the man, but that the sort of machine that is used is the decisive factor.

The machine does not weaken the capacities of the human body, but it weakens the capacity of the human mind. The machine does not weaken the capacity of the human body, because the muscles of the human body do not need human intelligence. The brain has no geometrical sense and no mechanical perception; and machines, as a rule, do not need a geometrical sense and a mechanical perception. Machines, as an example, do not need to know that a ball, dropped from the hand, will fall to the ground. To drop a ball from the hand requires no geometrical sense and no mechanical perception. This is why the machine does not weaken the muscles of the human body. But machines, as a rule, do need a human intelligence, as for instance, if the machine is to be used for the production of a new machine, or for some other purpose. Thus the machine does weaken the capacity of the human mind.
It does, because machines can do work that men can do, and thereby does away with the necessity for muscular effort, and hence renders the muscles less capable of effort.

Both are right. Machines do not weaken human capacities; rather, they multiply them. Machines do not weaken human capacities, for they do not do any work for which human muscles are equipped. Machines do not weaken human capacities; they do not undertake any activity for which human faculties are not equipped. Machines do not weaken human capacities; they do not perform any actions that are not within the compass of human faculties.

The question, in the form in which it is put, is ambiguous. If it is meant that the use of machines does not weaken the man who uses them, it is doubtless true that it does not. If it is meant that the invention of machines which are not used by the masses does not weaken the race, the answer is, yes, it does. The machine does not weaken the man who uses it, but it weakens immensely the race of men that does not use it.

We cannot say that it does not weaken human capacities. It is, for example, the displacement of the woodchopper by the power-boring machine that causes unemployment and misery. On the other hand, the use of machines is not without its benefits. The great increase in wealth, which has allowed a great development of culture, is due to the machine. Furthermore, the more man invents machines, the more his capacities will develop. In a sense, the machine is a means of liberating the capacities of man. The machine-mind is a product of the machine. The machine is a liberator. The machine is a liberator in the same way that the factory is a liberator. Both have liberated the human being from the slavery of manual labor. The machine-mind, as well as the factory-mind, is a machine-mind. The factory-mind is a machine-mind in the sense that it uses machines. The machine-mind is a machine-mind in the sense that it uses machines for the production of commodities. The machine-mind is a machine-m

If you use machinery to create new things you strengthen your capacities, but if you use it merely to perform a task which you were capable of performing without it, you weaken your capacities. The latter is what is happening with us. Some people are so foolish that they cannot understand that machinery in the hands of grown-up people is a luxury and not a necessity. They are the ones who rightly feel that they are

The first. For machines are not living things that have muscles and can tire. But men are living things, and have muscles that tire. Now you cannot tire things that are not living. You can tire men, but not machines. A man, by working desperately hard, can tire himself out, but he cannot tire out a machine. He can make a machine strain itself, but he cannot make it tire. In other words, a machine is not a living thing.

In abstracto, if we consider human nature to be constant, it is right to say that machines do not necessarily weaken human capacities. On the other hand, if we consider human nature, and especially the human mind, to be variable, we must say that machines do weaken human capacities. The difference between the two views is only a difference in the way we think of human nature; the difference is not an absolute difference. That which seems to be a universal truth, when we think of human nature in the abstract, becomes a particular truth, when we think of human nature in the concrete. From the last point of view we may say that machines do weaken human capacities. The question, therefore, is not one which can be answered by any set formula, but one which has to be answered by taking into account all the circumstances of the individual case.
Neither is right, for machines do not create powers; they merely liberate them. The powers remain the same, but they have a new domain.

The first statement is correct. If an individual depends on machines to do his work, he can not be said to weaken his capacities. But if he depends on machines for his daily bread, he does weaken his capacities, because it is clear that a machine can not support a human being. The second statement is wrong, because it is only by relying on machines that man can have leisure to devote to the improvement of his capacities.

The question is a very difficult one. It has been said by some that machines have a "deadening" effect on human capacity, and this view is not without support. It is supposed that the effect of machines is to dull the mind, by reducing the necessity for effort. But it is difficult to see how this can be true. A man who works with his hands, or who works with his legs, has to make a definite effort; but if his mind is employed, he can do a great deal without making any effort, and his mind may become more alert. If a man is employed in directing a machine, he has to use his mind, and is therefore in a better state than one who is merely doing manual labour. He is more alert, and what he does is more intelligent. But machines are often so automatic that they can be left for long periods without any mental effort being called for; and, as it is so much easier to work with machines than without them, the temptation is to leave them for long periods without any attention. So far, then, as the

The truth probably lies between the two views. No doubt it is true that the machine, by its unceasing demands on the mind and body of the worker, tends to make him incapable of any strenuous effort of his own. But the machine, on the other hand, by relieving the worker of the necessity of satisfying his wants directly by his own efforts, would seem to give him the opportunity of devoting himself to higher things, if only he values such things as highly as the necessary effort would imply. Here, as elsewhere, the question of value is the crucial one. For the man who values his own comforts above every other consideration, the machine is a curse. For the man who values his own self-development above every other consideration, the machine may be a blessing. The ultimate test is the state of mind of the worker.

The two views are both right and both wrong. Machines have both strengthened and weakened the human capacities. Their strength lies in the fact that they are efficient in a material sphere and give man immense power over nature; their weakness lies in the fact that they are not perfect, but subject to errors and accidents. As an example of what they have done for man, we may cite their application to the dynamo, which was invented in 1831. Before the advent of the dynamo industry was carried on by water-power, wind-power, and horse-power. The water-power could not be relied on to work all the year round, and it could not be applied to some industries. Wind-power could only be applied where the wind was a constant factor, such as on the coast. Horse-power was practically the only source of energy available in the city. The dynamo, which was applied to industry only a few years ago, has completely revolutionised industry and given us electric tramways, electric light, electric power, wireless, and so forth. Without the dynamo, half the industries of the world would be at

Both. A man who is fond of reading is strengthened by reading, and, at the same time, is weakened. He is weakened by the lack of exercise of his powers of observation, and strengthened by the fact that reading interests him and arouses his curiosity.

It is not possible to prove what is right or wrong in these matters. Machine production, like all the other means of production, is in the process of being modified. The Chinese had a remarkable system of irrigation, which Europe adopted without much change, but felt later that it was not up to date. We have begun to do the same thing with machines. It is not yet clear how we shall proceed.

Those who hold the former opinion are right. To rely on machines is to rely on that which is not living. Machines are the result of human labor and ingenuity; they are not living, and therefore they cannot be relied on for the future. It is for this reason that failure of machines is not rare; it means that human labor was not sufficiently intelligent to make them strong enough for the work they have to do. If we rely on machines we rely on something that is not living, and therefore we have no guarantee of the future.
Both are right. It depends on the individual.

We may hold that the develop ment of machines does not weaken human capacities, although they may never appear so prominently. Machines have been responsible for the present-day overcrowding and high rents, and have made the lives of those who have to live in them on a low standard of existence. The same criticism applies to the rapid growth of factories; but the first effect of factories on wages is to increase them. In the long run, however, factories have a degrading effect on the worker, because they are built in such a way that they are unhealthy places to live in. In a factory the worker is restricted in his movements and is dependent on mechanical power, and his work is often monotonous and mechanical. No wonder, then, that the factory workers are deteriorating physically and mentally. Machine-made goods have also a deteriorating effect on the worker; they are made on a low standard of living, and take the place of home-made goods which are made under better conditions. The result is that there are more people working at low rates, and the value of their services is thus reduced.

This question cannot be answered with any certainty. The great practical advantage of machines is that they save human labour. It is, therefore, quite clear that if the human labour thus saved is employed in other ways, the human capacities will not be weakened. They will only be saved from unnecessary drudgery. It is also clear that if the human labour thus saved is not employed in new ways, but is simply saved, the human capacities will be weakened. In fact, the question is one of the use made of labour-saving machines.

This depends on what we mean by human capacities. If we mean capacity to make machines, then it is true that mechanical invention tends to diminish the supply of such capacity. If we mean power to use machines, it may be that there is no such diminution. Certain it is that capacity for using machines is extensively cultivated, and that the supply of such capacity is steadily growing. This is shown, for example, in the spread in recent years of mechanical devices for housework, or in the spread of scientific management, where the introduction of motion study and the use of mechanical devices has increased enormously the output of men and women without overtaxing their physical strength. The same is true of the use of machinery in agriculture and in the industries. It is true of the use of machinery for transportation and communication. There is no doubt that the use of machinery, properly handled, is compatible with full human development for the worker.

The former is relatively right. The average man can do more work, can live longer, and can produce more wealth, than without the aid of machines. But machines do not improve the quality of his work. There is no room in the machine for an artist or a poet, and the machines take the place of the artist and the poet. The machine does not develop the creative capacity of the worker. And it is creative capacity that the world needs most.
Reliing on machines does not weaken human capacities.

The machine has the same effect on the human mind as an over-stimulating drug has on the body. The machine does not weaken the human mind, but it does for the time being render it unintelligent. In other words, the machine is a temporary substitute for intelligence. It is an artificial substitute for intelligence, and the use of it is equivalent to the use of a drug.

It is true that machines, among the things they do, do a great deal of work which does not call for the exercise of intelligence. It is also true that certain kinds of work can be done mechanically as well as by hand. But it is not true that the general effect of the machine is to do away with the necessity for intelligence. The fact is that the machine does not do away with intelligence; it merely enables intelligence to do more work. To say that the machine is taking the place of intelligence is nonsense. To say that intelligence is taking the place of the machine is sense. And that is exactly what is happening.

Those who hold the latter view are right. We are not machines. The machine is a device for doing work which we cannot do with our hands, heads, or bodies. We each have a soul; and this soul needs food, needs to grow. If our bodies are weak, our souls will not be strong. Machines are not real things; they are devices for doing things which we cannot do with our hands, heads, or bodies. Machines have no souls. Man has a soul, and this soul needs food, needs to grow.

Some hold that human capacities are weakened by specializing, but others hold that they are strengthened. The answer depends on whether the capacities are strengthened by the specialist's doing his work better than others or by his doing one thing all his life and that one thing poorly. The latter is certainly weakening. With respect to the former the evidence is conflicting.

Neither is right; both are wrong. A machine is not an instrument of thought; it is an instrument of dependence; it is the substitute for thought. All the thought that goes into it is spent in designing and in keeping it in repair; no thought is free to be spent on the thought-problems that are the true interest of man. It is not thought that gives the machine power; but a certain physical force, stored up by thought, and acting through the machine. All the time that you are thinking of the mechanism of your automobile you are storing up force to drive it. The man who relies upon the mechanism is in the position of the man who has not to work for his living; he is in the position of the man who has no social duties. This is a state of dependence, not a state of freedom. You cannot rise to the level of the machine, you cannot make yourself as mechanical as it is, and therefore you are not free. But you can fall to its level. The machine is an idealised form of dependence; it is the idealisation of a
It is not a question of whether machines weaken human capacities. They do, and they do not. The

The first view is held by advocates of "mechanisation" of industry, the latter is held by those who oppose it. The latter view is, of course, the correct one. For an example of the first view, see the following passage from an article by David L. Podell, "The Machine and the Man," in the New Republic (10-2-1935):

Both are right and both are wrong. Only when we make a right division of labour, only when we divide it according to the capacities of each individual, and when we, by machines, do what is done with difficulty by many hands, then is it right to employ machines and to use them in all possible ways. But if we employ machines when we could ourselves do the work, then we not only diminish our capacities but we also injure ourselves. This is true for all machines. But we should remember, on the other hand, that machines have their advantages too: they save time and labour, and make possible the production of many things which otherwise could not be produced. But if they serve only the production of things which cannot be produced without them, then machines are harmful. They are harmful when they deprive men of means of production and of productive labour. But they are harmful also when they take from men the production of things which are not necessary to human life, and which are used only for personal luxury. In both cases the machines serve only the needs of the rich and the comfort of the

It is true that machines can produce a great deal, but a machine cannot do everything, and, besides, a machine is always the same, and cannot adapt itself to changes in circumstances. It is very rare that one machine can replace another, as, for instance, in the case of a sewing machine, which can be replaced by a writing machine. In general the machines are able to replace only a part of our own capacity for work as regards the quantity produced (see p. 87). The most important objection to machines is this: machines, and especially small machines, working with the human faculties, such as telegraph or telephone machines, and machines for carrying letters, are very liable to get out of order. In such cases they have to be attended to by human labour. In this way the machines introduce a new kind of slave labour into the world, and this slave labour is more costly than the slave labour of our own kind, as it cannot be organised.
See the answer to the third question.

There is no contradiction here. The first assertion is true; the second is equally true. Both are true of different times, and of different individuals. The average man, who depends mostly on machines, is inferior, intellectually, to the average man of the time when machines were not so much used; but some men are superior to the average man in both respects. The introduction of machines does not necessarily reduce the average man, but it may and does reduce the superior man. To take an extreme case (though it is not an extreme one, at least with some people), the invention of the typewriter has reduced the average man to a lower level than he would otherwise have reached; but it has, on the other hand, raised many an individual to a higher level than he would otherwise have reached. Thus the average man has been reduced; the superior man has been raised. If we asked what effect the introduction of machines has had on the average man, we should be obliged to give it up; but we can easily see that, as a matter of fact, the average man has been reduced,

Those who hold that relying on machines weakens human capacities are right, because machines act upon us like the idols of the ancients, and like the gods of the heathen at the present day. The idols of the ancients were made to be worshipped by men; the gods of the heathen are worshipped by men. Both idols and gods were made by men, and were useful to them. Similarly, machines were invented by men and are useful to them. But, all the same, both idols and gods, as well as machines, tend to act upon us in such a way as to weaken our human capacities, our intellect and our will. Therefore, the more we rely upon machines, the weaker do we become in the faculties of the soul. This is exactly the same case as that of the man who, by giving himself up to gambling, becomes a gambler. The more he gambles, the greater a gambler does he become. The same is the case with the man who, by drinking too much, becomes a sot. The more he drinks, the greater a sot does he become. The same

They are both right, according to the point of view. If a man is a pure machine, his mind is weakened by being attached to a machine; if he is a living being, his mind is strengthened by being attached to a machine. If a man is a machine, he is no better, but worse, for helping to make machines, because he does not understand what he is doing; but if he is a living being, he is certainly better for helping to make machines, for he gains a knowledge of his own power and weakness. If a man is a machine, he is certainly better, but not so well, for improving machines, because he does not know what he is doing; but if he is a living being, he is certainly better for improving machines, because he learns his own power and weakness.

Both are right; for human capacities are dependent on machines; capacity is not independent of them. Machines do not weaken human capacities; they assist them. Machines do not make men stupid, but they make them clever. Machines do not make men weak, but they make them strong.

The first opinion is right if we consider human capacities in the light of their independent activity. The second opinion is right if we consider them in the light of their relation to the machines. While machines are increasing and men are becoming the slaves of machines, their capacities are weakened, and they are growing stupid. But if the machines are being brought under human control their capacities are being strengthened.

It is a matter of opinion, but the latter view is more likely to be true. The Italians, who seem to have been the first to use machinery in the western world, were a superior people, and the use of machinery has not interfered with the intellectual development of western Europe. But in the East, where machinery has been used from time immemorial, the peoples are inferior, and the use of machinery has not helped them.

It depends on what you mean by "machines." If you understand the machines to be the great apparatus of modern industry, then the former opinion is right; if you mean the inventions of machines and the employment of the machines for the purpose of saving labour, then the latter opinion is right. Machines, in the first sense, are the substitute of labour, and the labour is weakened; but if you understand machines in the second sense, then machines are the invention of men, and the men are not weakened by the machines that they have invented.

The question of human capacities depends on the purpose for which they are used. If one does not use his capacities so as to injure his neighbour, it is well. But if one uses his capacities so as to injure another, it is not well. In this case it is contrary to human capacities. The machine is useful for the human capacities, but the human capacities are injurious to the machine. The machine is for the use of the human capacities, while the human capacities are for the use of the machine. The use of the human capacities without injuring others is a good thing, but the use of them so as to injure others is a bad thing. If, with the machine, one can serve the human capacities without injuring others, it is well. But if, with the machine, one injures others, it is bad.

In so far as the machines work more rapidly than human workers, the work is performed by the machines. If this is so, it will not be held that the work is done by human workers. Where, then, is the weakness? The human workers would be free to do other work, and, therefore, their capacities would not be weakened. In so far as the machines work more slowly than human workers, the machines are not working and human workers are. If this is so, it will not be held that the work is performed by machines. Where, then, is the weakness? The machines would be working and human workers free to do other work, and, therefore, their capacities would not be weakened.

The machine is an instrument which contains within itself a force. This force can be applied and used by man, but he himself need not be present. It is quite natural that the machine should weaken the capacities of man, because it frees him from the necessity of using his capacity.

The former is right. Machines do not weaken men's capacities. Machines make men; machines are not made by men; machines are not the outcome of human ingenuity; machines are not the result of human invention. Machines are the creation of God. Man's function is to control, to guide, to regulate. Human capacities are strengthened by the use of machines.

The first is right. Just as the use of the bicycle or the motor-car has not lessened the vigor of the human body, so the use of machinery has not lessened the vigor of the human mind. The profoundest and most original thinkers in the world have been men of the machine age, as for example, Newton, Darwin, Edison, and others.

Both are right, according to the point of view. Both rely on machines, but not in the same way. The first rely on machines to do their business for them, and to relieve them of the necessity of troubling about it. They get their food and clothes from machines, but they do not overwork machines, thus weakening their own capacities. The other class rely on machines to help them to do more than they could do without machines. This is what people call work, which really means effort, and which weakens the capacities of the worker. This is what one sees in the poor people who work in factories, and is called the tendency of machines to "socialise labour," _i.e._ to deprive the worker of all initiative, of all chance of developing his own capacities, and of all responsibility. This is the real danger of machines to the worker. It is not the machines which deprive him of initiative, it is the _worker_ who relies on the machine to do his work for him, and to free him from the responsibility of deciding for himself.

All machines by their nature are artificial. A machine as such has no will, no desire, no thought. It only works mechanically, not like a human being, whose sole motive is a desire to be useful. Machines are thus something lifeless or dead. The natural consequence is that those who rely on machines to the extent of giving up their free will are themselves becoming dead. The fact that a machine is dead does not, however, prevent it from being used as a tool in certain cases. But the very fact of such use shows that human beings should not rely on machines except as tools. The best way of using machines is to make them serve our ends by being the servants of our will.

The second view is correct. Human capacity is weakened; but in such way that the loss is more than compensated by the gain. One may acquire the knack of using machines, but if he is to develop all his powers, he must learn to use machines intelligently and not mechanically. The mastery of machines is itself a great art, and requires some degree of intelligence. It is well known that machines may be so used as to make the workers more intelligent, as, for example, in the case of the Swiss watchmakers. The most intelligent workers are those who have developed the art of machine-tending in the highest degree, and who at the same time have retained the greatest amount of personal initiative.

It is a matter of opinion. The fact is that it is not a question of machines, but a question of machines and men together. When the machines are of a certain character, the men are not weakened by relying on them, and when the machines are of a different character, the men are weakened by relying on them. To understand which, we must understand the character of the machines. There are machines which do not weaken men but strengthen them, and there are machines which do not strengthen men but weaken them. The weakening of men through machinery is a consequence of the nature of the machinery. It is not a question of machines, but a question of machines and men together. In this way, in the case of the machines we have mentioned before, which are machines made by men and not by themselves, the machines do not weaken men. In the case of the machines made by themselves, the machines do weaken men.

Neither is right. Neither position is true. Machine-using is not necessarily an enemy of the human race: it may be used as a help to the race. In the first place, the machine is a device for making what we need. It is a means of making things more economically than they can be made by hand. The machine is an instrument for saving the human hand. The machine makes it possible to accomplish more for the advancement of mankind. It helps us in our work. It is an instrument of production. It is a tool.

The first are right. Machines take the place of human labour. In so far, therefore, as we employ them, we lessen the opportunities of labour. It is true that the invention of machines is a sign of increased humanity and a sign that we have more leisure and more intelligence; but the employment of machines to perform work that we can do ourselves, or can get done by human beings, is a sign of decreasing humanity and a sign that our intelligence is less than it ought to be. The more machines we invent, the more machines we employ, the less intelligent and human we shall become. We are now human beings, but we shall become inhuman machines.

Especially in the case of machines for performing mechanical operations, such as the typewriter and the adding machine, the human capacity to learn is called out in a way that would not be required if the machine were not there. The mastery of the machine also is an admirable training in observation and accuracy, and the human touch is not altogether eliminated by the machine. In the case of such machines as the piano, where the touch is a vital part of the performance, the machine does not train the capacity of the performer as much as the study of the piano.

Both are right, but neither is right. The truth is, that the development of the mechanical arts in conjunction with the development of the social arts and the development of science, has had an enormous influence in increasing human capacities in two principal ways: (1) by training the mind to accuracy and by the use of instruments of precision; (2) by providing the means of educating human faculties and training them to greater usefulness by the use of machines. It is probable that the human intellect has never been so active as it is at this moment. And it is certain that the mastery of the mechanical arts gives man a greater control over nature than he has ever had and puts more power into his hands. But it is a mistake to suppose that he is more helpless than he was before, because he has to depend more upon his own capacity. The truth is that the extension of the mechanical arts has given man more power in relation to nature, but that at the same time it has given him more power over himself. It has increased his control over nature; but it has increased his capacity for self-control

It is a question of the right use of machines. If used rightly, they do not weaken but strengthen us because they save our senses. The right use of machines is to utilize our brain power for the benefit of society; the wrong use of machines is to make slaves of us. The right use of machines is to make us free, the wrong use is to make us slaves.

It depends on how you regard such capacities. If you regard them as mere individual capacities, it is true that the human machine will be weakened. If you regard them as social capacities, then it is not true. The point is, that the greater the social development, the greater the individual development. The individual does not remain stationary. He either rises or falls. He is either made greater or less by the social process. For instance, in the old days of personal slavery, the slave was but a machine, and there was no individual development. In the new days of social slavery, the slave is but a machine, and there is no individual development. In the new days of social freedom, the slave is still a machine, but it is a machine that is developing. The machine is developing in a social direction, and that is the only development worth considering.

Both are right. The truth is that machinery does not weaken the capacities of those who use it, but it does weaken the capacities of those who do not use it. It is the same with books; to those who read them, they open new avenues of thought and give a new sense of power; but to those who do not read them they are only so much printed paper. So machinery to those who use it, increases their powers; but to those who do not use it, it only increases their helplessness and their dependence upon others. The machines of the future will be the servants of the people, not their masters.

It depends on the object in view. If machines are to be used as a means of reducing the amount of human labour, and thereby reducing the number of human beings required for a given amount of work, then it is right to say that reliance on machinery weakens human capacities. But if machines are to be used so as to relieve the strain on human capacities by getting useful work done rather more quickly, or rather more easily, than it can be done by human labour, then it is right to say that reliance on machinery does not weaken human capacities.

The first opinion is right, if you mean by machines such machines as are used now. The second opinion is right if you mean machines that will be invented later on. At present machines are mostly used for doing work that is done in its own nature monotonous and uninteresting. Consequently, machines do not give scope for, or make any demand on, the mental powers. Machines may be used in the future which will have demands on the mental powers. Perhaps, they will be used for production of goods which are now produced by hand. In such industries, machine work will be interesting because it will be varied and new, and it will call for mental powers. Then machines will develop and strengthen man's mental powers, and not weaken them.

This is a hard question to answer. It depends on the individual, and what he does. If he is a mathematician, a musician, or a poet, he may have his capacities strengthened by employing machines; and if he is a bricklayer, he may have them weakened. The machine does not make any difference to the machine, but it makes a difference to the human being. If he is a man of brains, he will have his brains sharpened by the use of machines; if he is a man of muscle, he may have his muscles weakened by the use of machines. It is difficult to say how it will be. It depends on the use to which the machine is put.

Machines are of three kinds—inventions, contrivances, and machines. Machines are inventions or contrivances, and machines are machines. Machines are inventions or contrivances, because they are made more or less as the human body is made, and are a combination of parts for the production of a certain effect. A machine is a machine, because, being a separate thing, it is not an invention or contrivance. The human body is an invention or contrivance because it is a combination of parts for the production of a certain effect. A man is not a machine, and a machine is not a man. Some men are machines, and some men are inventions or contrivances. Machines are inventions or contrivances, because they are made more or less as the human body is made, and are a combination of parts for the production of a certain effect. Machines are machines, because, being separate things, they are not inventions or contrivances. Machines are inventions or contrivances because they are a combination of parts for the production of a certain effect. Machines are not inventions or contrivances because they are separate things. Machines are inventions or contrivances

Though mechanism may serve us, it cannot be our master. The machine is the slave of man, but the man must remain the master. If it is not so, man is degraded and degraded not only physically but morally and intellectually. It is much better to have a man who is a good mechanic, than a machine that is a good man. Machinery can never be a substitute for man. It has never been a substitute for man, even in a factory, where it is said to have been most successful.

We are all agreed that in the past the human being has been weakened through relying on machines, because the machines have been too complicated for him to manage; but in the future, though he will still be dehumanized, he will be dehumanized in a different way. The machines will be less complicated, and he will be able to manage them easily; but he will not be able to manage them by himself. It will always be necessary to have a manager, who will be paid for doing it. This manager will be a skilled workman, but not necessarily a human being. He will be a human being, but not a conscious human being, and he will have to be trained in a special way for his job. He will have to be trained in a special way, because he will have to be trained to the human standard of behaviour, and to the human standard of human virtues. If the thing that is to be done is really necessary and important, it is a pity to weaken the capacity of men for doing it, but if the thing to be done is really unimportant, it is a pity to weaken the capacity of men for doing something better.

Let us see what this argument of the Socialists amounts to. They say, "We shall get rid of individual workers, and thus have more people who can enjoy themselves." This is a very common argument used by the Socialists. But I must say that I have heard a good many men who have worked hard all their lives and who have never had any chance of enjoying themselves, and who have been obliged to work all day long for their bread. How could they enjoy being Socialists? As a rule, they are the most miserable men I have ever met.
With the exception of the very few who have great talents, and whose work, therefore, would be a loss to the community, the less the machine has to do, the better the worker.

While it is true that human capacities have been developing more and more throughout the history of civilisation, and that the present is continually improving upon the past, it is also true that human capacities do not improve so rapidly when the conditions of living are increasingly made easy. Human capacities do not increase so rapidly as to keep pace with the increase in mechanical contrivances, and in consequence the mass of mankind is driven to more and more mechanical contrivances in order to make ends meet. In the end the greater the mechanical contrivances become the more and more dependent is the race of Man upon them.

Relying on machines may or may not weaken human capacities. If machines are used to do what is essentially the work of the human being, and if the machines are used for mechanical purposes only, they will not weaken human capacities. If machines are used to do things which are essentially the work of the human being, and if the machines are used for humanitarian purposes only, they will not weaken human capacities. But if machines are used for mechanical purposes without humanitarian purposes, they will weaken human capacities. If machines are used for humanitarian purposes without mechanical purposes, they will not weaken human capacities. In other words, if the machine is used to do work which is essentially the work of the human being, it will not weaken human capacities. If the machine is used to do work which is not essentially the work of the human being, it will weaken human capacities. Both parties are right. Machines do not weaken human capacities, but they direct them in new channels. They do not weaken but they change the nature of these capacities, and give them a new direction. The human capacities are not weakened, but their application is changed. They are no longer used for the production of goods for the consumption of the individual, but for the production of goods, not for the consumption of the individual, but for the use of all. The strength of human capacities is as great as ever. The change in the direction of their application is the only change. The human capacities are not weakened, but they are changed. This is the only right way.

The first is right. It is the tendency of the use of machines to weaken human capacities. It is the tendency of the use of machines to substitute the less intelligent for the more intelligent. This is true in spite of the fact that the use of machines helps to raise the general level of intelligence.

Both are right. We must distinguish between the individual and the race. The individual who is strong and self-reliant will be all the better for using machines, but the race will lose thereby. If the individual becomes dependent on machines, he will lack energy and initiative. If the race becomes dependent on machines, many will lose their initiative and many will be unable to get machines at all. The individual who uses machines will be the stronger for his experience. But the race which becomes dependent on machines will be weakened, and the individuals who cannot get machines will be less well off than those who can get them. Ultimately, it is the race that counts, not the individual. We must always bear in mind that the human race is an organic whole, and not a mere collection of individuals. It is the purpose of the race that really counts, not the purpose of the individual.

The first view is right. It is true that machines are often made to do things which human bodies do with natural ease. In the days when there were no machines, it was the custom to dig and carry earth with shovels and baskets carried on the shoulders. But in the Middle Ages, when machines were not known, the earth to be moved was carried in cradles, which were lifted off the ground and carried on the shoulders of men. In the same way the earth was carried to the top of the walls of a city, and the stones were carried to the top of the tower of the castle. In the days when the first machines were invented, it was the custom to carry the earth in baskets and to carry the stones in cradles. But now it is the custom to carry the earth in waggons and to carry the stones in waggons. So it is clear that machines have made work easier, and have made it possible to do many things without carrying earth in baskets or stones in cradles.
