The first statement is correct; the second is correct. Reliance on machines weakens human capacities in the same proportion as the machine eliminates the necessity of the human to exert his capacities, or in proportion to the number of machines he uses. Reliance on machines weakens human capacities in proportion as the machine is a substitute for the human. Reliance on machines strengthens human capacities in proportion as the machine is a complement of human capacities, or in proportion to the number of machines used by the human. It is, of course, true that in proportion as the machine is a substitute for the human, it weakens human capacities. This is one of the main reasons why the machines are hated, and why the human is at war with the machine. But it is also true that in proportion as the machine is a complement of the human, it strengthens human capacities. This is one of the reasons why the machine is loved and why the human is at peace with the machine.

The former are right. For instance, in the past, people of all nations used to rely on machines only when they were forced to do so. For example, the English used to rely on machines to perform their work only when they were not able to perform it by human labour. The result was that the English were not as efficient as they are now. Even at the present time, those who rely on machines are not as efficient as those who rely on their own labour. In the future, those who rely on machines will be in a worse position. At the present time machines are not used as much as they ought to be. On the contrary, they are used far too much. The result is that people are not as healthy as they ought to be. If people were to rely not only on machines but also on their own labour, then they would be more healthy than they are now.

Both are right and both are wrong. It depends upon the machines. The machine which weakens the human being is the machine which makes him a machine. The machine which does not weaken the human being is the one which does not make him a machine. There is no doubt that the application of machinery to human labour in the more mechanical branches of industry has done good to the worker. It has made him more skilful, more alert, and more intelligent. In the more intellectual branches of industry, such as medicine and law, machinery has done more harm than good. Americans are the most ingenious people in the world. Their inventions are more ingenious than those of any other nation. Yet the American is the most nervous, the most restless, and the least capable of continuous mental strain of any civilized people. He is a curious mixture of the savage and the machine. He has the cunning of the savage; he has the precision of the machine.
That is a question which is never likely to be settled. It depends on the individual, and on the whole, a machine is more likely to strengthen a feeble man than to weaken a strong one.

If a man relies on machines to do the thinking which he himself could do, then he is weakening his own capacities; but if he uses the machine as an aid to his own thinking, then he is not weakening his capacities. A man may be a master of typewriting, and be able to do much more work than a beginner. In the same way, a man may be a master of a machine, and be able to do much more work than a beginner.

Both are right. The capacity to work at all is a gift of nature; our method of work, mechanical or otherwise, depends on the kind of work we have to do. The machine does the work accurately, and saves us the trouble of looking after it; we can rely on it; and we are not forced to do anything that we do not like. As a machine, therefore, it is a great comfort.

If it be meant that the human hand is strengthened by inaction, then the first is right. But if it be meant that the human mind is strengthened by using its wits to overcome obstacles, then the second is right.

The man who wishes to be an inventor must, of course, rely on his own machine; he must have his own researches, his own laboratory, and his own experiments. The machine of which an inventor takes advantage must be his own handiwork. But the man who wishes to do creative work with his hands, as a sculptor, an architect, a mason, or a stonemason, does not require a machine for his work. The machine is a necessity for the inventor, but not for the artist.

The same argument applies to machines as to books and pictures, and indeed to everything in nature. It depends on the purpose for which the machine is used. In some cases machines are used to satisfy the brute needs of man; in other cases they are used to satisfy his intellectual needs. The former use is regarded as lower and more degrading than the latter. It is degrading to make a machine do the work of a man. The higher the machine is, the less degrading is its use. This is very clear in the case of a book, which is a machine for recording and preserving human thoughts and feelings. But there are books and books; and a book is higher or lower according to the use made of it. Thus, a book of arithmetic is, so far, a machine; and so is a book of cookery. But a book of Greek literature is higher than either of these; it is used to satisfy man's intellectual curiosity and love of beauty. We call the Greek book higher because it is used for a higher purpose. The same is true of pictures. A picture of a dead dog

Both are right. If, as they say, machines are the product of man's invention and should not be blamed for the deterioration of the race, we must remember that machines are the cause of the very deterioration itself. The invention of machines has deprived the people of work; and consequently unemployment has become chronic in most countries. The latter is certainly a very depressing influence on the human body and must weaken the human capacity. Thus the very machines which are supposed to be harmless, are proving themselves to be the cause of the deterioration of the race.

Both are right. It depends upon the individual. As a general rule it weakens human capacities and abilities, but there are individuals who are able to use machines without losing the human faculties they started with. These people are the exceptions. Most of us, however, are creatures of circumstances. If we installed machines and depended upon them, we would gradually lose our human faculties and abilities and become mere machines. Such a person would become a totally different person in course of time. He would become incapable of using his human faculties and abilities.

It depends upon what the capacities are. When the main work of a nation is done by machines, as a rule the people are not trained to depend upon themselves. But this is not the case in the United States. The American people, as a whole, do not trust entirely to machines. They have to rely on themselves because they are willing to do so. The machines help them out, but they do not relieve them of the necessity of thought and action.

Some say that machines are so much more efficient than human beings that man is made more efficient by using machines. Others say that machines are so powerful that they make man weak, inasmuch as he must rely upon them for support.

Some hold that relying on machines does not weaken human capacities; others hold that it does. Which is right? Let us consider. Machines are dumb, therefore they cannot reason nor command, nor will, nor think. They cannot, therefore, make a man weak. Machines are inert things, therefore they cannot make a man weak. Machines cannot see, therefore they cannot make a man weak. Machines cannot hear, therefore they cannot make a man weak. Machines cannot taste, therefore they cannot make a man weak. Machines cannot smell, therefore they cannot make a man weak. Machines cannot touch, therefore they cannot make a man weak. Machines cannot make a man weak. Therefore, relying on machines does not make a man weak. But there is another side to the question. Machines can work; they can produce, and by working they can make a man weak. Machines can destroy, and by destroying they can make a man weak. Machines can hurt, and by hurting they can make a man weak. Machines can kill, and by killing they can make a man weak. Both are right. Machines can help us, but they cannot take our place. Our minds and our hands must work, as always. The farmer will dig his ditches and plant his potatoes and use his hoe and his sickle just as ever, but he will do all this better and more quickly than before, because he uses the new machines. The farmer who does not use machines, but sticks to hand labour, is beaten in the race. The machine is the labourer's tool, not his master. The negro is physically the equal of the white man, under equal conditions. But the white man can develop himself, by using his brain, to twice the strength of the negro, who is content to use his muscles alone. Using machines does not weaken us; it helps us.

Machine-using does not weaken the capacity for thought; but it limits the need for it. The average man thinks little after he has mastered his machine. The inventor, on the other hand, has to think intensely in order to understand and improve his machine. That is why the inventor is more intelligent than the machine-user. But the machine-user is also more intelligent than the machine-user of the past.

The former view is right. That is, a man who does not rely on his own initiative, but on machines, is not weakened by so doing, but rather the opposite. The reason for this is that when an individual relies on something external to himself he can concentrate all his attention on his own work, which is what is called making a "feature" of it. If on the other hand he relies on himself, he is distracted by the thousand-and-one things that he must think about to keep himself and his work up to standard. (The "feature" man in the present article makes a "feature" of his work because he relies on machines; if he relied on himself, he would not be doing so.) Incidentally, he has an easy mind, because he is not worried by the fear that something will go wrong, or that he will be interrupted. The mind of the individual who relies on himself is constantly clouded by the fear that something will go wrong, or that he will be interrupted.
